intro: Extra virgin olive oil is not a quiet swap for palm or corn oil. It has a taste, and that taste ends up in the food.
This is a kitchen guide. Where it works in Malaysian cooking, how much to pour, what a pour costs at RM236 a litre, and when to reach for an infused bottle instead.

sections.heading: Is olive oil for cooking worth it in a Malaysian kitchen?

blocks.text: Yes, for most of what a Malaysian kitchen does daily. Tumis, roasting, marinades, rice and anything finished cold sit comfortably inside its range. Olive oil for cooking behaves differently from a neutral oil: it carries flavour instead of hiding, so use it where that flavour is wanted, and use less than you expect.
Where it fits less well is a wok on a hard flame. Heat limits are their own subject, and [what heat olive oil can take](/blog/olive-oil-smoke-point-what-heat-it-can-take) covers the numbers.

sections.heading: What changes when you cook with extra virgin

blocks.text: Three things change. The dish picks up a peppery, grassy note that a neutral oil never adds. Onions and garlic brown a little more slowly and more evenly. And quantity starts to matter, because a heavy hand tastes heavy: one tablespoon of a good oil reads as seasoning, three reads as a mistake.

items: **Flavour** — green, faintly bitter, with a peppery catch at the back of the throat.
**Colour** — vegetables roast to a deeper gold.
**Texture** — dressings cling instead of sliding off.
**Quantity** — start with half a neutral oil's measure.

sections.heading: Where olive oil for cooking works in Malaysian dishes

blocks.text: Everywhere the heat is moderate and the oil is meant to be tasted. Tumis for a sambal base or a plate of stir-fried sayur. Roasting ayam, potatoes, terung or pumpkin. Marinades for grilled fish. A spoon forked through rice once it has steamed. Salads, kerabu and ulam, where nothing is heated at all.

sections.heading: What does olive oil for cooking cost per dish?

blocks.text: Less than the shelf price suggests, because you pour teaspoons and tablespoons rather than cups. Arabian Village is **RM59.00 for 250 ml** and **RM103.00 for 500 ml**, which is RM236 and RM206 a litre. Divide by a thousand and a millilitre costs about 24 sen from the small bottle, 21 sen from the large.

blocks.text: Reach for the classic when the oil should not decide the dish: roasting, tumis, rice, a dressing you are seasoning yourself. Reach for an infusion when you want one clear flavour to arrive without chopping anything. The [Infused Collection](/products) is six botanicals in the same cold-pressed base, priced the same by size.

items: **Wild thyme** — roast potatoes, flatbread, a dipping bowl.

sections.heading: Buying and keeping a bottle you cook from every day

blocks.text: Buy the size you will finish in two or three months, then keep it away from the two things that age it fastest, heat and light. A dark bottle in a closed cupboard holds up far better than a clear one standing beside the hob in a kitchen that never really cools down.

items: Store it in a cupboard, not above the stove.
Close the cap after every pour. Air dulls it.
250 ml for a few times a week, 500 ml for daily cooking.
Fresh oil smells green and grassy; tired oil smells flat or waxy.

blocks.text: In Malaysia the brand is carried by **Berkat Madinah Store**, its official distributor, at Ampang Jaya and the larger Batu Caves branch in Prima Seri Gombak. Both open 8:00 am to midnight daily. [Where to buy](/shop) has the addresses.

conclusion.heading: Cook with it, do not save it

blocks.text: A bottle kept for special occasions goes stale before anyone gets to it. Olive oil for cooking earns its price on weeknights: the roasting tray, the tumis, the spoon forked through rice. Open the next bottle before the last runs dry.

faqs.q: Can I use extra virgin olive oil for everyday cooking?
faqs.a: Yes. Tumis, roasting, shallow pan work, marinades and cold dishes are all ordinary uses for it. The one place to think twice is sustained high-heat frying.

faqs.q: How much olive oil should I use per dish?
faqs.a: Roughly half what you would pour of a neutral oil. A tablespoon is enough to tumis for two, two tablespoons dress a roasting tray, a teaspoon finishes a plate.

faqs.q: Is cooking with olive oil expensive in Malaysia?
faqs.a: Per bottle it looks dear, per dish it is not. At RM236 a litre a tablespoon is about RM3.54, and about RM3.09 from the 500 ml bottle.

faqs.q: Can I use olive oil for tumis?
faqs.a: Yes, on a medium flame. Warm the pan, add the oil, then the onion and garlic. They colour more evenly than in a neutral oil, so allow an extra minute.

faqs.q: Should the infused oils be cooked with or only drizzled?
faqs.a: Both. They are culinary infusions in a cold-pressed base, so they roast and marinate like the classic oil. Their flavour reads clearest when the oil goes in late.

faqs.q: Where can I buy it in Malaysia?
faqs.a: From Berkat Madinah Store, the official distributor: its Ampang Jaya branch or the larger Batu Caves outlet in Prima Seri Gombak, plus its own Shopee and TikTok Shop counters.
